title: HOW MUCH TO SAVE: 6 THINGS TO KNOW
series_label: HOW MUCH TO SAVE FOR RETIREMENT: 6 THINGS TO KNOW

concepts.title: The 15% Rule
concepts.body: Save 15% of your gross income for retirement. It's the standard starting target — not magic, but a useful starting line. A 4% employer match counts toward that 15%, so an 11% personal contribution plus a 4% match hits the target.

visual_spec.callout_text: Save 15% of gross income. A 4% employer match counts — contribute 11% yourself and you hit 15% total.

concepts.title: Why 15% Works
concepts.body: At a 7% after-inflation return, $7,500 saved every year for 30 years grows to roughly $762,000 (IRS 2026 IRA limit × 30 years at 7%, hypothetical). The 15% rule is built on that same compounding arithmetic over a full career.

concepts.title: Your $1M Example
concepts.body: To reach $1,000,000 in 30 years with $10,000 saved today at 7%, you need about $753/month. That's roughly $281,000 of your own contributions — the other $719,000 is compounding. Same target at 5% needs $1,148/month; at 9%, $466/month.

concepts.title: The 4% Rule
concepts.body: Once you retire, the 4% rule says withdraw 4% of your portfolio in year one, then adjust that dollar amount for inflation each year. A $1,000,000 portfolio supports roughly $40,000/year. Rooted in the 1998 Trinity study of historical returns.

concepts.title: What Actually Matters
concepts.body: The number that matters is yours — based on your spending, not your income. A couple earning $120K but spending $70K needs far less than one spending every dollar. Use the Retirement Goal Calculator to turn your real target into a monthly amount.

concepts.title: Put It On Autopilot
concepts.body: Figure your target → calculate the monthly amount → automate it into your 401(k) and IRA. Get the match first (the cheapest money you'll ever get), then fund the IRA, then return to the 401(k). Run the calculator once; automate forever.

visual_spec.callout_text: Match first, then IRA, then back to 401(k). Automate the monthly amount — the math only works if you don't have to decide each month.

sources_footer: Sourced from IRS IR-2025-111, S&P 500 1928–2025, Trinity Study (1998), Vanguard VOO fact sheet
